A1-A2.headline: How Antibiotics Are Used On Farms Today

pages.text:
Farm drugs help treat sick animals and keep food safe to eat. Yet farm animals use 73 percent of all these drugs.

Heavy use makes germs grow strong, so key medicines stop working well for people and animals.
pages.caption: Germs move from farm animals to humans.

evidence.articleCaption: A CDC infographic on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria have the potential to spread from farm animals

pages.text: Years ago, farmers gave drugs to animals to help them grow very fast. Over time, countries passed strict rules to stop that habit. The European Union ended growth drugs in 2006. In 2017, the United States stopped farmers from using key human drugs to make animals grow bigger.

In 2017, the World Health Organization asked countries to cut drug use in food animals. Leaders wanted to slow down the danger of strong germs. Even so, money still pushes heavy use on crowded farms. Health experts warn that without real change, simple sicknesses could soon become very hard for doctors to cure.

To keep people safe, rules set clear wait times before meat or milk enters stores. That wait gives the body time to clear out medicine.

Scientists are testing new ways to keep animals healthy without heavy drugs. Those steps point toward cleaner farming for everyone.

B1-B2.headline: Managing Antibiotic Use Within Livestock Production

pages.text:
Antibiotics treat sick farm animals and help keep food safe. Yet livestock account for 73 percent of all global use.

Heavy farm use fuels drug resistance, weakening key medicines that both humans and animals rely on.
pages.caption: Drug resistance spreads from animals to humans.

evidence.articleCaption: A CDC infographic on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria have the potential to spread from farm animals

pages.text:
Farmers gave routine drugs to help animals grow faster and use feed. Regions tightened laws to curb that practice.

The European Union banned growth drugs in 2006. In 2017, the United States followed by barring medically important drugs for growth.

In 2017, WHO urged nations to reduce antibiotic use in food animals to slow rising resistance.

Cost pressures still drive heavy use on crowded farms.

Public health experts warn that without change, routine infections could become far harder to treat.

Laws require strict waiting periods before products reach markets. This pause ensures medicines leave the body first.

Researchers are testing safer alternatives that support natural health, offering a clear path toward sustainable farming.

pages.text:
Antimicrobials remain vital, yet livestock consume 73 percent of global supply.

Widespread agricultural use accelerates antimicrobial resistance, undermining clinical therapies.
pages.caption: Resistant bacteria migrate to humans.

evidence.articleCaption: A CDC infographic on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria have the potential to spread from farm animals

pages.text: Producers routinely administered subtherapeutic antibiotics to accelerate weight gain. Regulatory frameworks have gradually tightened in response. The European Union prohibited antibiotic growth promoters in 2006, and the United States followed in 2017.

In 2017, the World Health Organization advised curbing antimicrobial deployment to stem resistance. Economic incentives continue sustaining intensive usage. Specialists warn that inaction threatens a post-antibiotic trajectory where routine infections prove difficult to treat.

Consumer statutes mandate withdrawal periods before distribution, verifying residues clear tissues.

Researchers are developing non-antibiotic interventions that bolster immunity, charting resilient agricultural production.
